abstract: Chicago Fed Working Paper 2026-12 (July 2026) by Kristen Broady, Caleb Dunson and Anthony Barr is an ex-post check of automation-risk forecasts. It matches Frey and Osborne's (2017) computerization-risk scores and Tomlinson et al.'s (2025) Microsoft Copilot-based AI applicability scores to BLS OEWS employment and wage data for 2019-2024. The 38 occupations with the highest AI applicability scores (writing, editing, sales, customer service, programming, clerking) grew employment by 335,800 jobs, or 4.05 percent, and average wages by about 21.7 percent. The 35 lowest-applicability (mostly manual) occupations ended the period slightly below their 2019 employment level, with wages up about 25 percent. By Frey-Osborne risk, employment fell 3 percent in high-risk and 6 percent in moderate-risk occupations and rose 8 percent in low-risk ones, while wages rose in all groups. The authors conclude that exposure does not map mechanically onto job loss in the short run, and that exposure measures indicate occupational restructuring rather than forecast employment decline. Most of the window is before ChatGPT's release, so it says little about GenAI's effect after 2022.
keyFindings: Occupations with the highest AI applicability scores increased employment by 335,800 jobs, or 4.05 percent, between 2019 and 2024; employment peaked at 8.66 million in 2023 and slipped to 8.62 million in 2024.
Average annual wages in high-applicability occupations rose from $63,363 to $77,138 (about 21.7 percent) over 2019-2024.
Low-applicability occupations fell from 3,966,570 jobs in 2019 to 3,914,130 in 2024, still slightly below the 2019 level; their wages rose about 25 percent.
By Frey-Osborne risk: high-risk employment declined 3 percent, moderate-risk 6 percent, and low-risk rose 8 percent over 2019-2024.
Wages rose in every risk group: 26 percent (high), 21 percent (moderate), 22 percent (low).
methodology: Descriptive occupation-level comparison. Frey and Osborne (2017) risk probabilities (high >=0.70, moderate 0.30-0.699, low <0.30) and Tomlinson et al. (2025) AI applicability scores from 200,000 Copilot conversations in 2024, both matched via O*NET-SOC to BLS OEWS employment and annual wages, 2019-2024 (starting 2019 because of the 2018 SOC change). High/low applicability groups are the top and bottom 40 occupations in Tomlinson et al. that match Frey-Osborne (38 and 35 matched). US.
qualifiers: Tier 1 by repo convention for Federal Reserve working papers; not peer-reviewed. Caveats: descriptive, with no counterfactual or controls, so the changes are raw and not attributable to AI. The 2019-2024 window is dominated by the COVID shock and recovery; only 2023-2024 are post-ChatGPT, and high-applicability employment dipped slightly in 2024. Wages are nominal averages across a period of high inflation. The applicability groups are small (38 and 35 occupations), so they are not a representative slice of the workforce. The authors themselves say the risk scores are 'best understood as measures of technological exposure rather than linear predictions of employment decline'.
